Useful negative evidence for this languoid: (a) the only linguistic sections of Böhm 1975/1983 - Glottolog's Glottolog's most extensive description for Biem - are a grammar sketch and a wordlist of MANAM (1975: pp. 159-175, 177-240; 1983: pp. 305-326, 331-405), so the list of works to obtain hope of a Biem wordlist with accent marks in Böhm is much weaker than assumed; (b) Höltker 1937 is annotated '(Blupblup)' only; (c) the language index entry for Bam (Schouten Is; Biem?) cites, as far as the garbled the scanned textcan be read, only Ross 1988 an…

sources.citation: Ross, Malcolm D. 1991. How conservative are sedentary languages? Evidence from western Melanesia. In Robert Blust (ed.), Currents in Pacific linguistics: papers on Austronesian languages and ethnolinguistics in honour of George W. Grace, 433-451. Pacific Linguistics C-117. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-C117.433.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone (a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|penult|tone|tonal|prosod: 0 hits in 20 pp.). Bam figures only in shared-innovation tables and fn. 4: 'Phonologically, Bam is more conservative than Manam by one innovation, since it retains the Proto Oceanic/proto Schouten distinction between *n and *n~ (Table 1, innovation 8) where Manam has a merger. Morphosyntactically, however, Bam is considerably more innovative than Manam.'
